cultivar: Wuyuan local landrace with some Fuding Dabai
processing: Pan-fired then baked green: shoots are fired, rolled into a fine curve with the down raised, and dried gently, giving a slender eyebrow-shaped leaf.
harvest_season: Spring, from late March to late April; pre-Qingming and yu qian lots of a bud with one or two leaves.
appearance_dry: Slender, slightly curved, downy twists like eyebrows, deep green.
appearance_wet: Even bud-and-leaf sets, tender and bright green.
taste_profile: Sweet and thick with chestnut and orchid, a savoury middle and a long, clean sweetness.

brewing.notes: Gaiwan or glass at 80–85 °C. A forgiving, sturdy green; four steeps is normal.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring harvest, picked before Qingming or before Grain Rain. Plainer Wuyuan green is sold by export grade with no season, and much Wuyuan tea is marketed with organic certification. Drink within the year, kept cold and sealed.
description:
Wuyuan Ming Mei is the premium green of Wuyuan county in north-eastern Jiangxi, historically part of the Huizhou tea country that also gave the world Keemun and Tunlü. Wuyuan green has long been an export tea, mostly as anonymous Chun Mee grades; Ming Mei, 'tea eyebrow', is the named, finer style that shows what the county's leaf can do. It is often said to date from the late 1950s, though the record is thin.

It is made with a pan-firing followed by careful rolling into a slender curve and a gentle final drying that keeps the down, so the dry leaf looks like a finer, greener, fuzzier version of the eyebrow-shaped export tea it descends from.

In the cup it is sweet and quite thick: chestnut and orchid, a savoury middle and a long, clean sweetness, with more body than the Zhejiang bud teas and less roast than Anhui's. It is forgiving to brew, happy at 80–85 °C in a gaiwan, and good for four steeps. If a green from this region tastes smoky or sour, it is the export grade, not Ming Mei.

Wuyuan is well known for certified organic green tea, so Ming Mei and plain Wuyuan green may arrive with organic certificates, which is one reason the county's tea shows up in Western shops under generic names. Ming Mei proper is sold as the current year's spring tea; the plainer tea is sold by export grade with no season. Look for slender, downy, even leaf and ask for the picking date.

Wuyuan in late March, when the rapeseed fields bloom around the whitewashed Huizhou-style villages, is one of the prettiest places in China to drink the new tea.
sources_note: No dedicated English Wikipedia article found. Creation date 'late 1950s' follows Chinese sources (1958 is commonly cited).
history:
Wuyuan, in north-eastern Jiangxi, has a long green tea record, and the making of Wuyuan green tea entered China's national intangible heritage list in 2014. That listing belongs to the county's tea as a whole and not to Ming Mei in particular.

The date Ming Mei first appeared is poorly documented. It is often placed in the late 1950s, without a firm record behind that date. What is clear is its present definition: a 2024 group standard describes an eyebrow-shaped green made from the county's local population bushes and similar, fired, rolled, pan-dried a second time, shaped and finished.
